info.name: Viatuta API
info.description:
Viatuta is a cycling route planner that optimises for **safety first**, not distance or time. This collection covers every HTTP endpoint currently wired into the server (`internal/httpapi/server.go`).

**Current surface (Phase 1-4):**
- `GET /healthz` — liveness probe
- `GET /readyz` — readiness probe (DB + routing graph)
- `POST /v1/route/plan` — compute a safety-optimised route

Accounts, saved routes, and hazard reports (Phases 5-6) are stubbed out in the router source as commented-out routes and are **not yet live** — see the "Planned (not yet implemented)" folder for what's coming, kept here so this collection stays a complete map of the API surface as it grows.

### Error shape
Every failure returns the same JSON envelope (`internal/httpapi/errors.go`):
```json
{
  "code": "bad_request",
  "message": "human-readable explanation",
  "details": { "field": "what's wrong with it" }
}
```
`code` is one of: `bad_request`, `unauthorized`, `forbidden`, `not_found`, `conflict`, `internal_error`, `unroutable`.

### Rider profiles
`profile` selects a built-in weighting for the cost function (`internal/safety/profile.go`):

| Profile | max_lts | stress_budget_m | max_detour_ratio | Character |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `cautious` | 2 | 400 | 2.5 | Riding with children. Refuses anything above LTS 2 except brief forced crossings; will detour far for physical separation. |
| `comfortable` (default) | 3 | 800 | 1.8 | Prefers bike facilities, tolerates quiet streets, avoids arterials without a bike lane. |
| `confident` | 4 | 2000 | — | Will take a painted bike lane on an arterial to save real time. |
| `shortest` | 4 | 0 | 1.0 | Pure distance routing — the baseline every other profile is measured against. |

Pass `custom` instead of (or alongside) `profile` to override every weight per-request — no redeploy needed.

item.name: Operational
item.description: Health and readiness checks. Neither requires auth or a body.

request.description:
Reports that the process is alive and able to handle HTTP at all.

Deliberately does **not** check the database or routing graph — a liveness probe answers "should this process be restarted?", and restarting the API will not fix a down database, it will just add an outage. Use `/readyz` for dependency checks.

**No parameters.**

Response fields:
- `status` — always `"ok"` if the process responded at all.
- `uptime` — Go duration string since process start, e.g. `"42s"`.

Reports whether the process can actually serve traffic: pings the database and checks that the in-memory routing graph has finished loading. Use this as the target for a Kubernetes/load-balancer readiness probe — send traffic only once this returns 200.

**No parameters.**

Response fields:
- `status` — `"ok"`, `"starting"` (graph still loading), or `"degraded"` (database unreachable).
- `uptime` — Go duration string since process start.
- `database` — `"ok"` or `"unreachable"`.
- `graph` — `"ok"` or `"not loaded"`.
- `nodes` / `edges` — size of the loaded routing graph (only present once loaded), from `make ingest`.

item.name: Routing
item.description: The core product: computing a safety-optimised bicycle route between waypoints.

request.description:
Computes a route through the requested waypoints using the built-in `comfortable` profile — the default if `profile` is omitted entirely. Coverage is Austin, TX only.

**Body parameters** (`internal/httpapi/route_handler.go: PlanRequest`):
- `waypoints` (required, array of `{lat, lon}`, 2-10 points) — the origin, any via points, and the destination in order. Each point is snapped to the nearest rideable road; `-90<=lat<=90`, `-180<=lon<=180`.
- `profile` (optional string) — one of `cautious`, `comfortable` (default), `confident`, `shortest`. Ignored if `custom` is set.
- `custom` (optional object) — a full weight override; see the "Custom Profile" request in this folder for its shape. Mutually exclusive in effect with `profile` (custom wins if present).
- `night` (optional bool, default `false`) — enables the lighting penalty for unlit roads, on top of whichever profile/custom weights are used.

A 3+ waypoint request is planned leg-by-leg (waypoint 1→2, 2→3, ...); the per-leg results are concatenated, and note the stress budget applies **per leg**, not across the whole trip.

**Response: `segments`**
Alongside the flat `geometry` LineString, the response carries a `segments` array saying WHERE each of the `breakdown` distances happened. Each entry is a run of consecutive roads sharing the same traffic stress and facility type:
- `start` / `end` index `geometry.coordinates`. `end` is **inclusive** and equals the next segment's `start` — consecutive runs share that junction vertex, so slice `[start, end+1]` to get polylines that join up.
- `lts` is 1-4, or 0 for a road `viatuta score-edges` has not classified. Note this is a NUMBER, whereas `breakdown.by_lts_m` uses string keys (`lts3`).
- `infra` uses the same vocabulary as `breakdown.by_infra_m` keys.
- `length_m` sums the roads in the run; the segment totals per `lts` agree with `breakdown.by_lts_m` to within rounding.

Runs are merged rather than emitted one per edge — a 97-edge route typically collapses to a handful of segments.

The `cautious` built-in profile: modelled on riding with children. `max_lts: 2`, `stress_budget_m: 400` — it will accept a long detour (`max_detour_ratio: 2.5`) in exchange for physical separation from traffic, and only tolerates 400m total above LTS 2 across the route (e.g. one bad block, not ten).

Same body shape as the default request; only `profile` differs. Expect a longer, safer, more circuitous `geometry` and a higher `detour_ratio` than `comfortable` for the same waypoints.

The `confident` built-in profile: an experienced rider who will take a painted bike lane on an arterial to save real time. `max_lts: 4`, `stress_budget_m: 2000`, low weights across the board so the cost function stays close to raw distance while still preferring safer edges when they're roughly as direct.

The `shortest` built-in profile: pure distance routing, ignoring safety entirely (`max_detour_ratio: 1.0`, no stress budget, all weights zero). This is the same distance-only search the server internally uses to compute `baseline_distance_m` / `baseline_safety_score` / `detour_ratio` for every other profile's response — request it directly to see that baseline as the primary route.

Overrides every cost-function weight for this single request — no redeploy, no built-in profile needed. If `custom` is present, `profile` is ignored (`internal/httpapi/route_handler.go: resolveProfile`).

**`custom` fields** (`internal/safety/profile.go: Profile`), all required unless noted:
- `name` (optional string) — a label for the response's echoed `profile.name`; defaults to `"custom"` if omitted.
- `max_lts` (int, 1-4) — the highest Level of Traffic Stress this rider will use *without* dipping into the stress budget. LTS1 = protected/quiet, LTS4 = arterial with no separation.
- `stress_budget_m` (float, meters, >= 0) — total distance above `max_lts` tolerated across the whole route. `0` makes `max_lts` a hard wall — the router will report `unroutable` rather than ever crossing it.
- `weight_lts` (float, >= 0) — multiplier on traffic-stress cost. Higher = stronger preference for low-stress roads.
- `weight_crash` (float, >= 0) — multiplier on historical crash-pressure cost for an edge.
- `weight_grade` (float, >= 0) — multiplier on hill/elevation-grade cost.
- `weight_surface` (float, >= 0) — multiplier on road-surface-quality cost (e.g. gravel vs. pavement).
- `weight_light` (float, >= 0) — multiplier on the unlit-road penalty; only has an effect when `night: true` (or the top-level `night` request field is set).
- `weight_turn` (float, >= 0) — multiplier on turn cost (unprotected left turns, crossing traffic, etc.).
- `max_detour_ratio` (float) — only used to decide whether to attach a `warnings` message on the response; does not affect routing itself.
- `night` (optional bool) — same effect as the top-level `night` field; the two are OR'd together.

All weights must be `>= 0` (a negative weight would make an edge cheaper than its own length, breaking the router's invariants) and `max_lts` must be in `[1,4]`, or the server responds `400 bad_request`.

`night: true` turns on the lighting penalty (weighted by `weight_light`) on top of whichever profile is selected, biasing the route toward lit roads. Combine with any `profile` or `custom` body — it's an independent flag, not a profile of its own.

`waypoints` accepts 2-10 points; anything beyond origin/destination is a via point the route is forced through. Each consecutive pair (1→2, 2→3, ...) is routed as an independent leg and concatenated (`internal/httpapi/route_handler.go: routeLegs`) — meaning the stress budget resets per leg. `snapped` in the response will contain one entry per waypoint, in order, so you can see how far each requested point was moved to reach a rideable road.

item.name: Plan Route — Error: too few waypoints (400)

request.description: Demonstrates the validation error returned when fewer than 2 waypoints are supplied — an origin and destination are both required (`internal/httpapi/route_handler.go: validWaypoints`).

response.name: 400 Bad Request — waypoints

request.description: Demonstrates the error returned for a `profile` value that isn't one of `cautious`, `comfortable`, `confident`, `shortest` (`internal/safety/profile.go: ProfileByName`).

response.name: 400 Bad Request — profile

item.name: Plan Route — Error: no route within stress budget (422)

request.description: `max_lts: 1` with `stress_budget_m: 0` makes LTS1 a hard wall — no crossing of any higher-stress edge is permitted at all. If no all-LTS1 path connects the waypoints (common in Austin, where the low-stress network is islanded by arterials), the router returns `422 unroutable` instead of silently relaxing the constraint. This is the deliberate design described in the README: a rider who set a stress budget must never be handed an arterial without being told.

response.name: 422 Unprocessable Entity — unroutable

item.name: Plan Route — Error: no rideable road nearby (422)

request.description: Demonstrates the error when a waypoint is outside Austin coverage (or otherwise has no nearby routable road for the snapper to attach to). `(0,0)` — off the coast of West Africa — is a convenient always-fails example.

item.name: Hazards
item.description:
Rider-reported hazards, as a live overlay on the safety model. Unlike crash records and elevation — which are refreshed by a batch job — a hazard affects routing immediately: the handler rebuilds the in-memory overlay before it responds (`internal/httpapi/hazard_handler.go`).

Reports are accepted anonymously. Sending a Bearer token records you as the author (`optionalAuth`), but is never required.

request.description:
Submit a hazard at a point.

**Body** (`internal/hazard/store.go: Submission`):
- `location` (required, `{lat, lon}`) — where the hazard is.
- `kind` (required string) — one of `debris`, `pothole`, `poor_visibility`, `aggressive_traffic`, `blocked_lane`, `construction`, `dangerous_junction`, `other`. These match the CHECK constraint on `hazard_report.kind`.
- `notes` (optional string, max 500 chars).

Note the field names are `kind` and `notes` — not `type` and `description`. The server decodes with `DisallowUnknownFields`, so a wrong name is a 400 rather than a silently ignored field.

A hazard reaches 30 m in every direction (`hazard.MatchRadiusM`) — wider than the crash radius, because a rider dropping a pin from memory is less precise than a police report filed at a known intersection. Reports expire after 90 days.

item.name: List Hazards in a Bounding Box

query.description: Required. minLon,minLat,maxLon,maxLat — the order is longitude-first, matching GeoJSON rather than the {lat, lon} objects used in request bodies.

request.description:
Active hazards inside a bounding box. `bbox` is **required** — there is no unbounded listing.

Returns `{"hazards": [...], "count": N}`. Each report carries `id`, `location`, `kind`, `notes`, `confirmations`, `created_at`, and `expires_at`.

Record corroboration from another rider, which increases the hazard's weight in the cost function. Returns the updated report.

Returns `404 not_found` if the id is unknown or the report has expired.
